draft.title: The solubility product
card: A slightly soluble salt in water forms a saturated solution. The solid and its dissolved ions are at equilibrium, for example: PbI2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2I-(aq).

The solubility product, Ksp, is the equilibrium constant for this dissolving. The solid is left out of the expression, so Ksp = [Pb2+][I-]2. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.
To find solubility, let s be the moles of salt that dissolve per litre. For PbI2, [Pb2+] = s and [I-] = 2s, so Ksp = s × (2s)2 = 4s3.
Ksp is also used as a limit. Comparing the ion concentrations in a mixture with Ksp shows whether a precipitate will form.
draft.remember: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for a salt dissolving, written with the ion concentrations only.

a.q: Which expression is the Ksp for calcium fluoride, CaF2(s) ⇌ Ca2+(aq) + 2F-(aq)?
a.why: Ksp uses only the dissolved ions, and each is raised to the power of its coefficient, so fluoride is squared. The solid is not included, so dividing by CaF2 is wrong.
a.clue: Leave out the solid and use the coefficients as powers.

b.q: Silver chromate, Ag2CrO4, has a molar solubility of s mol/L. Which expression gives its Ksp?
b.why: Ag2CrO4 gives [Ag+] = 2s and [CrO4 2-] = s. So Ksp = (2s)2 × s = 4s3. Using 2s3 forgets to square the 2 in 2s.
b.clue: Square the silver concentration, which is 2s.
